problem: Standard imitation learning needs expert actions (kinesthetic teaching or teleoperation) for every new task. Prior visual-imitation work either hand-defines a state to infer from images, which breaks under perception errors, or uses plain inverse dynamics models (Nair et al. 2017). Those models are trained with a delta-target cross-entropy that suffers when many actions or trajectories lead to the same next state, and they cannot decide how many steps a sub-goal needs.
motivation: Showing a robot *what* to do with a sparse sequence of images is much cheaper than showing it *how* with state-action pairs, and the same demonstration mode works for many tasks. The driving observation is that for most tasks reaching the goal matters more than the exact actions. Penalizing predicted actions that differ from the explored action but have the same effect injects high-variance gradients, and this worsens with trajectory length.
key_idea: Learn a goal-conditioned skill policy (GSP) purely from the agent's own self-supervised exploration, using hindsight goal relabeling. Train it with a forward-consistency loss: a learned forward model must map the GSP's predicted action to the same next observation or feature as the ground-truth action. At test time, a separate goal recognizer lets the robot follow a sparse image-only expert demonstration landmark by landmark.
insight: Scoring actions by their predicted consequences instead of their identity handles action multi-modality without generative modeling. The GSP-FwdRegularizer ablation is the clearest evidence: a forward model used only as a feature regularizer does well on the training map with new textures (median 50.6) but overfits and drops to 37.9 on a new map. The consistency loss reaches 44.8 (pixels) and 47.1 (features) there, so the gain is not just regularization. Data quality also matters. Curiosity-driven exploration data beats random exploration for every model (e.g. new-map median 39.1 to 47.1 for the feature-space GSP), and on TurtleBot, previous-action history (2 to 4 of 8 successes) and forward consistency (4 to 6 of 8) each add successes.
method: Self-supervised exploration + hindsight relabeling: the agent explores with no expert (random actions on TurtleBot and Baxter, random or curiosity/ICM policy in VizDoom); visited states are relabeled as goals and executed actions become prediction targets.

Goal-conditioned skill policy (GSP): a recurrent network takes φ(current obs), φ(goal obs), previous action a_{t-1} and hidden state, and outputs a_t autoregressively. It is a variable-step generalization of an inverse dynamics model, trained with action cross-entropy.

Forward consistency loss: a forward model f(φ(x_t), a) is trained on GT transitions (||φ(x_{t+1}) − f(φ(x_t),a_t)||²). A second term λ||φ(x_{t+1}) − f(φ(x_t), â_t)||² pushes the GSP's predicted action to have the same effect as the GT action. The forward model and GSP are pre-trained separately (gradient blocked), then fine-tuned jointly; λ ≈ 0.1, or picked from {0.01, 0.05, 0.1} on validation in VizDoom.
Feature-space dynamics: consistency is computed in a CNN feature space φ (learned via action prediction) rather than raw pixels. Used in VizDoom; raw observation space is used on the real robots.

Goal recognizer: a separate goal-conditioned binary classifier decides whether the current obs is close to the goal. Positives are observations a few actions from a pseudo-goal drawn from exploration; negatives are beyond a margin. It beat adding a 'stop' action.

Visual imitation at inference: given sparse demo images (every 5th frame on TurtleBot, every 10th in VizDoom), the agent runs the GSP toward landmark i until the goal recognizer fires or a step cap is hit, then switches to landmark i+1.

setting.backbone: TurtleBot: ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 + recurrent GSP (fine-tuned); Baxter rope: pretrained AlexNet + non-recurrent skill head; VizDoom: CNN encoder φ + recurrent GSP trained from scratch on 42x42 grayscale; plus learned forward model and goal recognizer
setting.training_data: Only self-supervised exploration data, with no expert actions and no rewards. TurtleBot: 230K (x_t,a_t,x_{t+1}) interactions from random exploration on two floors of an academic building. Baxter: ~60K random pick-and-place interactions (Nair et al. 2017 data). VizDoom: 1.5M frames each of random and curiosity-driven (ICM) exploration on the DoomMyWayHome map (action repeat 4).
setting.observation: monocular RGB (TurtleBot Orbbec Astra camera); 42x42 grayscale single frame (VizDoom); top-down RGB of the rope (Baxter); goal given as expert-demo images
setting.action_space: TurtleBot: discrete {forward ~10 cm, turn left/right ~14-18°, no-op}; VizDoom: discrete actions with action repeat 4; Baxter: pick-and-place primitive (grasp point, direction, displacement length)
setting.simulator: VizDoom (plus real-world TurtleBot2 office navigation and Baxter rope manipulation)
setting.privileged: none (the task is specified only by a sequence of first-person expert demonstration images; no expert actions, map or pose)

The VizDoom split mapping is my own: 'Same Map, Same Texture' = training env → val-seen, 'Same Map, Diff Texture' = validation → val, 'Diff Map, Diff Texture' = zero-shot generalization → test-unseen. VizDoom ± confidence intervals / standard errors are omitted from metrics. Real-robot evaluations are small bespoke setups (8 goal-finding runs, 3 runs per demonstration), not standard benchmarks.
results: Forward-consistent GSP raises knot-tying success from 36% (inverse model of Nair et al. 2017) to 60% on Baxter. On TurtleBot in an unseen office floor, it reaches single-image goals in 6/8 runs, versus 0/8 for random search and the inverse model and 4/8 for GSP-NoFwdConst. It follows sparse (every 5th frame) demonstrations where SIFT matching reaches only 5-15% of landmarks and ORB-SLAM2 fails to build a map, completing 2/3 loop runs where GSP-NoFwdConst reaches 0%. In VizDoom, curiosity-driven exploration data improves all models, and on a novel map with novel textures the feature-space GSP reaches a median completion of 47.1%, versus 40.2% for GSP-NoFwdConst and 37.9% for GSP-FwdRegularizer.
limitations: Skill quality is bounded by exploration data: random exploration on the real robot never crosses rooms, so far goals need dense intermediate landmark images.
Requires first-person demonstrations and assumes matching visual statistics between demo and execution; loop demos under different lighting failed for all models.

Very small-scale real-world evaluation (a handful of runs, bespoke metrics). Efficiency gains are inconsistent: the feature-space GSP has the lowest efficiency on the new VizDoom map with curiosity data.
